| [NOTE-132](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-132.md) v2 | Moral disciplining: foundations of puritanical morality | Puritanical norms (condemning lust, gluttony, intoxicants, immodesty, idleness; praising temperance and piety) are argued to be cooperative morality after all: people believe cooperation needs self-control and that indulgence erodes it (and discipline trains it), so a single harm/fairness-sensitive moral system condemns victimless pleasures as indirect, probabilistic threats to cooperation. | [NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md) | The moral psychology of obligation | Tomasello proposes that the human sense of obligation is "the internalized social/rational pressure from a joint or collective self-regulating agent 'we'… to do what 'we' expect me to" (§3). | [NOTE-403](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-403.md) | Haidt 2001, the social intuitionist model | The social intuitionist model: moral judgments appear in consciousness as quick intuitions with an affective valence, and moral reasoning is usually a post-hoc search for supporting reasons, used to persuade others. | [NOTE-405](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-405.md) | Rai & Fiske 2011, relationship regulation | A theoretical review. Moral psychology is the regulation of social relationships: an act is right or wrong according to the relational model participants and observers apply, not according to its harm, fairness or purity in the abstract. Fiske's four models (communal sharing, authority ranking, equality matching, market pricing) each carry a moral motive: Unity, Hierarchy, Equality, Proportionality. Honour killing, obedient massacre, blood feud and collateral damage are each read as one motive at work. Purity and ingroup loyalty are both Unity. No new data are reported. | Read |

| [NOTE-407](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-407.md) | Baumard, André & Sperber 2013, mutualistic morality | Partner choice with outside options constrains how the gains of cooperation are split: nobody accepts less than they could get elsewhere, so with equal options the stable split is proportional to each partner's contribution of effort and talent. Twenty-eight commentators accept partner choice and dispute that fairness is all of morality; the authors reply with a broad and a narrow position they have not settled between them. | Read |
| [NOTE-408](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-408.md) | Curry 2016, morality as cooperation: a problem-centred approach | The founding statement of morality-as-cooperation. | [NOTE-1267](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1267.md) | Population ethical intuitions | Nine experiments with US online samples. People require more happiness than suffering for a population to be better existing than not (about 75% happy; about 61% when the two are stated to be equally intense). Yet they judge adding one extremely happy person as good as adding one extremely unhappy person is bad: they reject the intuition of neutrality and the procreation asymmetry. With averages fixed they prefer larger happy and smaller unhappy populations, but the preference for more happy people fades and, at a billion against ten billion, reverses. With totals fixed they prefer higher averages. In conflicts averagism tends to win, to the point of preferring to add near-maximally unhappy people who raise the average. Prompts to reflect move judgements toward totalism. | Read |
| [NOTE-1270](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1270.md) | The Psychology of Existential Risk: Moral Judgments about Human Extinction | Parfit's three outcomes, put to laypeople: no catastrophe, 80% of humanity killed, 100% killed. More do when the victims are zebras (44%, 35%), when the catastrophe sterilizes rather than kills (47%, 29%), or when reminded that only extinction ends humanity's future (50%, 39%).
